Interviewer: Okay. So my name is Jackie Smith. I work at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, and I am interviewing Mr. Peter Miller on October 3, 2012 over the telephone. Can you — can we begin by having you state your birth name.
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: Your place of birth and your date of birth.
Interviewee: Yes. My birth name was Jack Peter Miller.
Interviewer: Okay. And you —
Interviewee: It was December the 1st, 1928.
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: And the rest of the, the parents?
Interviewer: Where were you born?
Interviewee: In Budapest, Hungary.
Interviewer: Okay, and what were your parents' names and dates of birth, if you remember?
Interviewee: My parent — my father was David Miller, his birth, he was born in 1897.
Interviewer: Where?
Interviewee: In Horadenka.
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: That's Poland at that time. And my mother's name was Lisa Miller, with the same birth date, and she was born in Budapest, Hungary.
Interviewer: Okay. And did you have any siblings?
Interviewee: Yes. I have a brother, Connor Matthew Miller.
Interviewer: And when was he born?
Interviewee: He was born in 1929, December the 18th.
Interviewer: Also in Budapest?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: Yes. And what — when did your family move to Budapest? When did your father move?
Interviewee: When he was a baby.
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: I don't know, at age one, I think, or one and a half.
Interviewer: Okay, so the family was firmly based in Budapest?
Interviewee: Yes, yes, yes. He served in the Austro-Hungarian Army during the first world war.
Interviewer: Okay, and what language or languages were spoken in your home?
Interviewee: Hungarian.
Interviewer: Just Hungarian?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: And did all of your immediate family, meaning your brother and your parents and yourself, survive the Holocaust?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: And did your extended family, grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousins, did they also live in Budapest?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: And were they —
Interviewee: Well, there were some in the United States.
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: There were some in, we found out, in Switzerland. There was somebody in Romania. There were others. A couple of them were in England.
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: As a matter of fact, my grandfather's — there were seven brothers, and two of the brothers went to Palestine in the 1800's.
Interviewer: And did, so did grandparents and uncles, were they involved in your life in Budapest?
Interviewee: Well, only up to a point because they passed away when both my brother and I were quite young.
Interviewer: Okay, okay.
Interviewee: As a matter of fact, I was named after one of my grandfathers.
Interviewer: Okay. And what did your parents do for a living?
Interviewee: My father was the foremost jeweler in Budapest, was decorated at an international exhibition by Prince Joseph from the Habsburg Court, and he was given the equivalent at that time Master of the Gold, of the Golden Wreath. That would have been an equivalent to being knighted in England and being called "sir".
Interviewer: Okay. And what kind of jewelry did he make?
Interviewee: He was making — of course, in those days it was all fine handmade jewelry, and he designed them all, and he had all the, the nobility and the, and the stars from movie and theater as his customers.
Interviewer: Okay, and so would you have considered your family pretty well off?
Interviewee: At the time we did not know. My parents did, never divulged what they were worth, for the right reasons, because later on it was proven that the Hungarian police and the Nazis were picking up children and giving them candy and chocolate and asking them a lot of questions about the parents.
Interviewer: Okay. To try and find out where the money was?
Interviewee: Right, exactly.
Interviewer: Right. And did you have, did you have household maids or servants?
Interviewee: Yes, we did: we did, yes.
Interviewer: And was your family religious?
Interviewee: Conservative.
Interviewer: Okay. And did you receive religious instruction?
Interviewee: Yes. We went to a Jewish elementary school and a Jewish gymnasium.
Interviewer: Okay. And what do you recall about your relations with non-Jews? Obviously your father had customers who weren't Jewish
Interviewee: Yes, of course: but my relation was, and my brother's, only that when we were beaten up by other kids on the street because we were so identifiable because of the emblem of our school, gymnasium on our caps
Interviewer: Okay, so that —-
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: — you definitely experienced.
Interviewee: It was never, it was not a amicable encounter.
Interviewer: Okay, and was the neighborhood that you lived in, was it —
Interviewee: It was the central —
Interviewer: — a Jewish neighborhood?
Interviewee: No, it was the central part of Budapest.
Interviewer: What street was it?
Interviewee: It was the H-A-J-O Street.
Interviewer: Okay. And what synagogue did you go to?
Interviewee: We went to the — well, it's what's called the Rumbach.
Interviewer: Sure.
Interviewee: If you've heard about it.
Interviewer: Um-hm.
Interviewee: Yes. And sometimes to the Dohany, the largest one in Budapest.
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: But mostly to the Rumbach, and that's where both my brother and I were bar mitzvahhed.
Interviewer: Okay, and did you, did you — did your family attend services regularly?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: Okay. So, so obviously your, you know, you suffered at the hands of anti-Semitic school children?
Interviewee: Well, yes, I mean.
Interviewer: And what about on a political level, were you old enough to be aware of —-
Interviewee: No.
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: No. The only thing that I — I mean, I knew that they were electing people to parliament, but I mean from what party or who they were, I really did not, no.
Interviewer: And did you feel anything from your parents that they were worried as things got worse or —
Interviewee: Yes, yes, yes, yes. My father was quite — well, he, he was cognizant of the fact what was going on starting in 1938, and later on there were refugees coming from Poland, and he was one of the places they came for funds to help them go to, to Italy or, you know, leave the country.
Interviewer: Okay, so he helped.
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: He helped, yeah.
Interviewee: Yes, yes.
Interviewer: But he — did you feel like your family felt that there was any imminent threat in Hungary?
Interviewee: When?
Interviewer: Well, from — you know, as Germany sort of expanded and started taking over other countries?
Interviewee: Well, only inasmuch that the Hungarian government, an ally of the Nazis, was bringing in laws that would curtail Jewish activities like attending college —-
Interviewer: Right.
Interviewee: — becoming a doctor or engineer. They had a very, very small percentage that they accepted, only the top, top students, and later on that too was done away with.
Interviewer: Right, right. And were you aware of the Arrow Cross?
Interviewee: Oh, yes.
Interviewer: Yeah. And, and —
Interviewee: As a matter of fact, they were marching many times under our windows.
Interviewer: Okay, and so I assume you feared them and, and —
Interviewee: Well, I mean, you know, at that time that was the, way before the war, we didn't fear them because they were not, they did not have any real power —
Interviewer: Right.
Interviewee: — because just the demonstrations that they — the same thing like the Ku Klux Klan has done here.
Interviewer: Um-hm.
Interviewee: You know.
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: You didn't want to get in their way and you didn't want to face them: but, no, we were not particularly scared —
Interviewer: Right.
Interviewee: — at that time.
Interviewer: And so how much did you know, how many details did you or your family know about the treatment that Jews were receiving -
Interviewee: Oh, that we knew, that we knew.
Interviewer: — in Germany?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: You knew about Kristallnacht?
Interviewee: Well, at that time we did not know about Kristallnacht, but we knew about what was going on in Germany because, you know, at the dinner table these things were discussed—
Interviewer: Um-hm.
Interviewee: — and mentioned, and so we were — I mean, we didn't really — my brother was 13, I was 14 at the time, so, you know, we did not, we were busy with our own activities —
Interviewer: Concerns.
Interviewee: — more or less: and, but, yes, we were aware because we belonged to the Boy Scouts, but we could not be called Boy Scouts.
Interviewer: Okay. Okay, because —
Interviewee: Because there was no such thing as a Jewish Boy Scout
Interviewer: Okay, okay, and, but at that point your family didn't consider trying to immigrate or —
Interviewee: Yes, my father did. Oh, it was in 19 — in 1934, I think if I'm correct, he did get an American visa,
